arceus: Arceus is the god of Pokemon and for good reason. It has 120 in every stat and the ability to change type based on what plate it holds. It has a signature move Judgement that is a 100 power special attack that matches the type of the plate it is holding as well. Arceus has an extremely deep move pool that even includes Palkia’s signature Spacial Rend alongside Tailwind and Trick Room. At 120 speed, it is one of the fastest Tailwind users and screen setters. This is kind of the perfect draft league pokemon with its immense power matched by its immense versatility. Giving up an item slot is usually a price worth paying for getting an incredibly strong and bulky pokemon of any type you want, but if not, normal is a fairly good type to begin with. Arceus should almost undoubtedly be picked first overall.
palkia: Outside of Arceus, Palkia is my personal pick for strongest available Pokemon. Water and Dragon typing gives it only two weaknesses to fairy and dragon, combined with numerous resistances for incredible defensive typing. This combined with Palkia’s strong bulk and Fairy being a very uncommon type in Gen4 means that Palkia will be very difficult to remove before it tears through opposing teams. It boasts an absolutely absurd 150 special attack alongside strong coverage options and an incredible signature move in Spacial Rend. In its base form, Palkia has a very respectable 100 speed and 120 attack to allow it to play as a physical attacker if needed. Origin Form gives even more flexibility by allowing Palkia to sacrifice an item slot to reach an incredibly fast 120 speed while sacrificing its attack stat.
cresselia: Man, I’ve been waiting to talk about this one. I won’t beat around the bush. Cresselia is the best Trick Room setter of all time. With so many pokemon in this pool benefitting tremendously from Trick Room, it would be incredibly wise to draft Cresselia as soon as you get the chance. I don’t call it the best Trick Room setter of all time lightly either. Porygon2, Dusclops, Oranguru, Farigiraf, they all wish they were Cresselia. Sure, it doesn’t have a fancy ability or a synergistic typing, but I’ll tell you what it does have- monstrous, disgusting, impenetrable levels of bulk. If Cresselia were hit by an 18-wheeler going 90mph on I-85, the truck would flip on its head and cause a 20-car pileup, and Cresselia would just use Lunar Blessing and be fine. 120 HP, 110 Defense, and 120 Special Defense. It’s an amazing pokemon regardless of what kind of team it’s on, but being able to set Trick Room while being nigh impossible to one-shot makes it particularly suited to that role. But with 85 speed, it can just as well provide speed control on a faster team with Icy Wind. It can use Ally Switch, Helping Hand, Set Screens, etc, but the main event is Lunar Blessing. Dawg, this move heals 25% of its own and its ally’s health, works through protect, AND removes status effects. I know Arceus and Darkrai make good arguments for being 1st pick overall but to be honest, I’d respect the hell out of you for picking Cresselia instead. I’d also hate you because playing against this pokemon is an absolute nightmare. Nothing can outstall this thing. You can’t even poison it to death because it’ll just cure it. It can set up with Calm Mind all it wants and eventually start doing damage. It has all the time in the world. Alls I’m saying is if you wanna take down the Cresselia team, you’d better be packing some serious heat. And maybe some sleeping moves…
dialga: Before I bury the lead, Dialga is a good Pokemon– not quite an all-time great, but certainly one of the strongest Pokemon in this draft pool. It will absolutely be selected in the first round, and very likely to be drafted in the first 4 picks. Dragon/ Steel is a fantastic typing with an insane 9 resistances and 1 immunity and great type synergy. Steel neutralizes dragon’s weaknesses to Fairy and Ice, while Dragon neutralizes Steel’s weakness to Fire. With 100 or more in HP, and both defenses, Dialga will be hard to take down quickly. Its only two weaknesses in Fighting and Ground both usually hit on the physical side– Dialga’s better defensive stat. Offensively, it is fantastic with 150 base special attack threatening huge damage on basically everyone with its solid coverage move pool. So, if it is so great, why only in the top 4? Well, the number 1 spot goes to Arceus and it isn’t close. And Dialga is likely worse than its Pearl counterpart due to being slower and having a worse signature move. Also, rounding out the top 3 is Heatran who has a mega which is just a giant ball of stats. So… fourth. Just missed the podium. Dialga’s signature move, Roar of Time, is single-target, only 90% accurate…for some reason… and needs a recharge turn. That means it needs to rely on Dragon Pulse and Flash Cannon for STAB. These are solid moves, but hardly befitting a restricted legendary. Again, it is a really good Pokemon, but just not as good as its peers.
heatran: Heatran is fucking goated. It may no longer be the best grass type of all time since the removal of tera types, but it’s still a damn force of nature, man. Flash Fire is an incredible ability and it will make your opponents think twice about launching a fire type attack of any kind into any slot when Heatran could switch in at any moment. But Heatran is not amazing because of its ability, it’s because it’s a fire-steel type (the only one ever) and its 106 defensive stats and 91 HP make it extremely hard to kill without a ground type move (to which it is 4x weak). Also it has 130 Special Attack. Now, 77 Speed is terrible, but the bulk more than makes up for that. Fire-steel resists normal, flying, psychic, and dragon, 4x resists bug, grass, ice, fairy, AND steel, and is immune to poison. I’d say that more than makes up for its 2 weaknesses to water and fighting and its 4x weakness to ground. This pokemon’s moveset is a work of art, too. Any fire type move you can think of, Heatran has it, along with coverage moves like Earth Power, Dragon Pulse, Dark Pulse, and Solar Beam. Its signature move, Magma Storm, is a 100 base power fire type move that traps the opponent and damages them over time, but it is only 75% accurate, which kinda makes it dogshit tbh. Heatran even has a few support options in Taunt and Will-O-Wisp. And if that wasn’t enough, it also gets Iron Defense + Body Press, which could be pretty annoying on a pokemon this hard to kill. I will say, though, it bears repeating just how big a problem ground types are for this pokemon. The only coverage move it has that hits ground for super effective is Solar Beam, which needs sun active to be usable. So just be wary of that. Otherwise, near-perfect pokemon. If it’s not drafted in the 1st round, we are fools. This is like 3rd overall pick material.
shaymin: Shaymin rocks! Specifically, Sky forme. Regular Shaymin is fine. Sky Shaymin hits 127 speed, making it the fastest non-mega and only outsped by Mega Lopunny. Plus it gets tailwind so that makes it the fastest Tailwind setter. And that's not all! Shaymin has a powerful 120 special attack and the ability Serene Grace. It can hit hard and fast with Air Slash while also imposing a 60% chance of flinching on its target. And there's even more! Shaymin gets a Signature move Seed Flare which is massively powerful 120 power special attack with, after Serene Grace, an 80% chance to lower the target's special defense by 2 entire stages! It does have the downside of being only 85% accurate which means there are a lot of rolls that need to go in your favor but it's relatively likely? This basically means Shaymin can set up itself and its allies while also pumping massive damage. Few targets will survive two rounds with Shaymin on the field. I should mention normal shaymin as it has 100 in all stats making it quite bulky and it can fill a bit more supportive role. It gets all the same moves so that means seed flare and tailwind are still on the table.
darkrai: The coldest motherfucker in gen 4 isn’t an ice type- it’s my boy Darkrai. 125 Speed and 135 Special Attack is already pretty insane but add to it 70 HP and 90 Defense and Special Defense and you’ve got a solid stat distribution for a somewhat bulky, fast, special sweeper. Everyone knows Darkrai’s main draw is its signature move- Dark Void. But here’s the tricky thing… I’m not sure if Dark Void is going to function how it has in the past in this draft league or not. See, historically, Dark Void has been a spread move that puts both opposing pokemon to sleep. They nerfed it to only be 50% accurate, but it’s still pretty valuable regardless, especially with Darkrai’s ability Bad Dreams chipping ⅛ of all sleeping pokemon’s HP. Dream Eater pairs nicely with this. However comma, in Legends Z-A, they changed Dark Void to be a 60 power spread move that inflicts drowsy instead of sleep. It also has the special effect of doing double damage to the target if it’s already drowsy. This means not switching out after you’re hit with it will be punished severely. I could see a Darkrai with choice specs easily 2-shotting both opponents with this in the right circumstances. But again, that’s just how the move functions in Z-A, which isn’t a mainline game. It’s safe to assume they’re going to change it to work that way going forward but I don’t think we can use that version of the move yet on showdown. But either way, Darkrai is and has always been a fantastic support and special attacker, one which absolutely deserves top 3 picks overall, probably top 2. With such a unique supportive function along with a fast Taunt, Disable, Haze, Snarl, and Icy Wind, its utility cannot be denied. But its offensive movepool is pretty deep too. Thunderbolt, Ice Beam, Sludge Bomb, Psychic… Did you know it also learns Palkia’s signature move- Spacial Rend? I just found that out! What the fuck?
lopunny: Mega Lopunny is a top-tier Faker Outer. If you draft Lopunny, you must use its mega form to get much out of it. It’s absolutely worth it though. Mega evolving makes it a normal/fighting type and gives it Scrappy, which is a phenomenal ability that allows it to hit ghost types with normal and fighting type moves. Plus, its mega form has 136 Attack and 135 Speed, so it’s a serious menace. I’ve never seen a pokemon do more damage with Fake Out than Mega Lopunny. From there, the world is your oyster. This thing gets coverage moves out the wazoo and even a good amount of support options such as Fake Tears, Encore, Helping Hand, Thunder Wave, After You, and Toxic. Plus, you even have some nice utility in Drain Punch, U-Turn, Circle Throw, Power-Up Punch, etc. DRAFT THIS POKEMON! IT’S REALLY GOOD!
togekiss: Togekiss is one of the strongest redirection supports in the game. It boasts a (rare in Gen4) Fairy typing, access to Follow Me and Tailwind, and incredible abilities in Super Luck and Serene Grace. It can heal itself via Soft-Boiled or allies with Life Dew, hinder foes with Thunder Wave, Yawn, and Screens, or function as an attacker with an impressive 120 special attack. It has the bulk to function as a strong support and the speed and offensive stats to be a threatening special attacker. With Serene Grace its STAB Air Slash boasts a frustrating 60% chance to flinch whoever it hits. Togekiss is among the best supports available in this draft and should not drop beyond the 2nd round.
manaphy: Infamous for being one of the hardest shiny hunts of any pokemon. You need to have a copy of Pokemon Ranger, play the entirety of that game plus bonus post-game missions, just to get a Manaphy egg. Oh, and there is only one egg PER COPY of Pokemon Ranger–not per save… per cartridge. Seriously. How’s the pokemon? Really good actually! As we have seen in previous draft leagues, Pokemon with 100 across the board has shown to be very good. Solid, versatile stats are incredibly valuable in a format where you can tailor your team every week. Exactly two moves push Manaphy from good, to a great pick: Tail Glow and Heart Swap. Tail Glow is an extremely rare move which boosts special attack by three stages. For those playing at home, a three stage boost means the special attack stat is multiplied by 2.5x. Great start, but it gets better. With Heart Swap, Manaphy can transfer those stat changes to ally pokemon already on the field. If you are careful with your speed stats, you can give your attacker a 2.5x power boost on the same turn they attack. Heart Swap works by swapping stat changes with the target. An opponent boosts up too much? Heart Swap. Your ally clicked Draco Meteor and now has lowered special attack? Heart Swap. It is a crazy powerful move to enable other pokemon on your team. Not that it needs the help. It has access to STAB Scald, and coverage in Psychic, Energy Ball, Shadow Ball, Ice Beam, and Alluring Voice. It can hit basically every pokemon for neutral damage and after a Tail Glow, that is going to hurt. Special attention should be paid to Stored Power which gets boosted two ways with Tail Glow. Synergy! With great versatility, strong offensives, and incredible support options, Manaphy is a high-tier pick. It shouldn’t go later than the 2nd round.
giratina: This is an all-timer right here. I love Giratina so much, but is it the best competitively? Not really. However, I still think it’s worth making your first pick if the other powerful legendaries are gone. Ghost-dragon is not the best typing, as there’s no defensive synergy to speak of, but it’s not bad typing by any means. The Telepathy ability gives you immunity to allies’ attacks like Earthquake, so that’s always useful. Of course, you also have Levitate so you’d probably just use that. It already resists Surf and Discharge so yeah, idk why you would use Telepathy lmao. Anywhooo, Giratina is a split attacker, which is kind of neat, since it’s hard to prepare for. Its stats are perfectly symmetrical and its 2 forms swap the offenses for the defenses. 100 and 120, with base form favoring defense and origin form favoring attack. 150 HP and 90 Speed on both. Origin Forme is definitely the better of the two since 150 HP and 100 in both defenses is still super tanky. However, it might be worth it to stick with base form since Origin requires an item. You do get access to Calm Mind so setup is on the table. Having that versatility does make it a good draft league pokemon but it’s nothing crazy.
froslass: Frosslass should be used more or less exclusively in its extremely powerful mega form. Frosslass is very fast, reasonably bulky, especially in Snow, and in its mega form threatens for big spread damage via Blizzard. It can set its own snow which it may then utilize to set Aurora Veil support, offer speed control via Icy Wind, or damage via Blizzard. At 120 speed, only a handful of pokemon can match or outspeed it, and the support it offers the team on top of being a fast offensive threat means you will never regret having Frosslass on your team. It is perhaps the strongest mega on the board and should be picked up in the 2nd round.
gallade: Gallade is a powerful physical attacker with high special bulk and a strong Mega form to play with. Its base form is somewhat slow and physically frail, but the mega form shores up the physical defense a bit and hits an impressive 110 speed. It also gains access to Inner Focus which will protect it from Intimidate and Fake Out and, perhaps most importantly, it gets a terrifying 165 attack stat. Base Gallade gets Sharpness which allows it to hit very hard with Psycho Cut and Sacred Sword as well as Justified which can be paired with something like Beat-Up to allow Gallade to stack multiple attack boosts. Gallade is stacked with tons of coverage and support options. Coaching, Disable, Ally Switch, Trick Room, Destiny Bond, Encore, Heal Pulse, Screens, Taunt, Wide Guard, Will-O-Wisp, Icy Wind, and Thunder Wave form an impressive lineup of options and that’s just the less obscure ones. Gallade has excellent offensive coverage with Rock Slide, X-Scissor, Leaf Blade, and more. Shadow Sneak offers a Priority option when needed. Combine this depth of utility with a powerful and fast mega form and you have one of the strongest picks in this draft. Gallade is a clear high tier pick and should be picked up in the 2nd or 3rd round.
bronzong: Pretty solid! I could see this pokemon being picked round 2, maybe round 3. It has a good defensive profile and two solid abilities to keep your opponent guessing. Levitate gets rid of the ground weakness and Heatproof cuts fire damage in half. You can pick the one you think will be more likely based on your team and what your foe might run, and you have the benefit of the unknown. Since you could have either, your opponent might not want to hit you with any fire or ground moves since they might just end up wasting a turn. Since Bronzong does get STAB on Heavy Slam, there is a small reason to consider the ability, Heavy Metal to get the most out of it… but don’t. It probably isn’t worth it. Still, it has a good number of tricks it can pull like both screens and Imprison. With a few strong megas running around, Skill Swap might be good too. It can do enough to fit on most teams well.
garchomp: This has gotta be my and most everyone else’s favorite gen 4 pokemon. In terms of the overlap between aesthetic appeal and competitive viability, it’s arguably the best-designed pokemon of all time. Garchomp’s whole deal is that it’s extremely strong, very fast, and formidably bulky all at the same time. Its Achilles’ Heel is the 4x weakness to ice, which sure betrays how bulky it truly is, given how easy it feels to remove it from the board because of it. God help you if you’re running MEGA Garchomp, as that makes you unable to run Yache berry, which you’ll basically always need in this counter-team-ass context.But I digress. Provided you’re not just sticking it with Yache berry, Garchomp can make use of a lot of different items. I’ve had fun using Rocky Helmet with Rough Skin to get extra chip damage on physical attackers with a strategic switch. Assault Vest is always good since this pokemon is built to launch tons of coverage moves like Rock Slide, Iron Head, Poison Jab, and the like. And of course, it has access to plenty of good special attacks if you want to run Mega Garchomp for some reason. I like to rag on Mega Garchomp and it’s really just because I feel losing 10 points in speed and gaining so much Special Attack is kind of a waste and getting stuck with the Sand Force ability locks you into a very specific kind of mode. That said, if you are running a sand team (like, say, if you wanna draft Hippowdon), you’d be a fool not to go for Garchomp. The aforementioned Sand Force combined with the ungodly 170 Attack makes you an absolute beast if you mega evolve. But even if you don’t, Sand Veil is a reasonably annoying strategy to employ if you like gambling, giving all attacks a 20% chance to just miss you. You could combine that with Bright Powder to bring it up to about 30% and become a true piece of shit. Though, I will say I have tried this before in Pokemon Champions and it’s not as consistent as it sounds tbh. Most of the time, Garchomp benefits most from simply having Life Orb to increase damage output or Assault Vest to allow it to live longer. (But really just use Yache Berry)
weavile: They were really cooking when they designed Weavile. They really said “What if Sneasel was a baller?” and that’s how Weavile was conceived. It would not be the final answer to that question, but that’s a story for another day. Anyway, Weavile has a whopping 120 Attack and 125 Speed. It’s the definition of a glass cannon, but for my money, it’s just about the best one you’re gonna find outside of Mega Lopunny. Having used it for a time in Pokemon Champions, I can attest that there’s rarely a lead where it doesn’t threaten something in a huge way with a very powerful Knock-Off. Low Kick gives it an edge against heavy things like Rhyperior, Rampardos, Bastiodon, and Probopass. Plus, it can use Fake-Out to great effect, even against an opposing Fake-Out user given its high speed tier, unless that opposing Pokemon happens to be a rabbit wearing ripped leggings. But aside from that, Weavile is a great Pokemon. Draft it early on for an excellent Fake-Out user and a perfect answer to Froslass, Garchomp, Torterra, Hippowdon, and more! Just be sure to give it a sash.
staraptor: What a glow up. As one of the most exciting new megas introduced in Z-A, Staraptor has a bunch of shenanigans it can pull. Firstly, it gets access to ‘intimidate,’ making it one of only 2 Sinnoh lines blessed with the ability. Additionally, it has access to the third fastest tailwind in the format, only behind Shaymin Sky, and Arceus. With access to tailwind, sun, rain, and U-turn, Staraptor– even without mega– can function as a decent support. If you don’t care about sacrificing your own pokemon, you can also use it as a fast ‘Final Gambit’ user. With a decent 85 base HP, the move threatens a one-shot on threats like Darkrai, Lucario, Gallade, Bronzong, and notably Lopunny. Killing yourself has never been so effective. If you still have a zeal for life, Mega Staraptor can do its bread-and-butter: spam ‘close combat.’ Not only is Mega Staraptor fast at base 110, with ‘Contrary’ each use of ‘close combat’ will boost both defenses by 1 stage. If you’re feeling spicy, you can even use a stat lowering move into your own Mega Staraptor to give it additional boosts. ‘Scary Face’ now gives +2 speed, ‘Charm’ now acts like a free ‘Swords Dance.’ While it might be a bit fragile at first, once it gets going, it can be extremely difficult to stop. A great pick for round 2 onward.
uxie: Azelf is more damage-focused, Mesprit is an all-arounder, and Uxie is fully built for bulk. It’s not going to be doing a ton of damage with its 75 base Attack and Special Attack, but what it will do is support its team and be hard to remove with its 75 HP and 130 Defense and Special Defense. Also, Uxie gets Yawn. So there you have it folks, Uxie is the best of the lake trio. It can really take a beating, set itself up with Nasty Plot (and Amnesia, which the others don’t get), and support the team with Yawn, Helping Hand, screens, and Encore. Good pokemon I think.
azelf: Before looking it up, I was like many people and completely unable to discern the difference between the lake trio. They all have the same typing, ability, stat total, and mostly the same movepool. Where they get their identity is in their stat spread. Azelf is the fast offensive one– meaning it is likely the 2nd best of the trio. To be clear: 115 speed, and 125 in both attacks is pretty solid. With a deep supportive move pool and the speed to move before almost anyone, you can do all sorts of BS. While it isn’t as fast as Prankster, because it isn’t, that means Azelf can target dark-types with Encores, Taunts, and Tricks to ruin their plans. If you want to go on the offensive, it gets Nasty Plot to boost up, Draining Kiss, and a respectable range of coverage options. It has two different pivoting options in Baton Pass and U-turn. I think the spirit of… Bulbapedia says Lake Valor…will likely be a really solid secondary attacker for your team. It has enough depth to be tweaked to most matchups, with the stats to back that up. I think this will be a sleeper hit that will only become more annoying as the season goes on. I would personally start looking at this blue guy in round 3, though you might be able to get it at a bargain in round 4, with some luck.
lucario: This is a great value pick. Not many Pokemon get two megas to play with, and Lucario has two solid options. Firstly, the base form. It is a decent mixed attacker, but you aren’t picking this for the base form. Mega Lucario Classic™ gets the great ability in Adaptability. With a fairly fast 112 base speed, and the option of running a physical or special set, you can dish out a bunch of damage. While you aren’t the bulkiest around, physical attackers need to worry far less about Intimidate, as it is much more rare this time around. Solid all around, if nothing too special.
rotomwash: This is just a solid Pokemon. If you play any Pokemon Champions, you will know how versatile and annoying this stupid washing machine is. Firstly, this thing is bulky. Don’t let the 50 base HP fool you, with 107 base in both defenses, and only one single weakness, Rotom - Wash can really take a hit. It is even better since it has some useful resistances in common attacking types like fire, water, and ice. Offensively, it is no slouch either with a really meaty 105 base special attack. So, it can work as an attacker, it is usually played as a bulky support which just happens to be able to dish out damage. A common set is using Choice Scarf to outspeed key threats, get speed control with Electroweb, or pivot out with Volt Switch. Just this dance, made even more annoying if you grab one of the few Intimidate ‘mons, can be worthwhile. With a modest list of solid supportive options like Will-O-Wisp, Thunder Wave, and both screens, it can slot onto a team really well. Offensively, it has fewer options, notably its only water move is the inaccurate Hydro Pump. But with a Pokemon this generally good, and versatile enough to fit on most teams, I’d imagine it finds a place somewhere in the high 3rd round.
rotomheat: Electric-fire is actually insanely good typing when you have the ability Levitate. You’re only weak to rock and water, and water types are weak to electric, so there you go. I don’t think there’s another pokemon in existence that gets this much value out of having Levitate, because otherwise, the 4x weakness to ground would be seriously detrimental to this mon. Its only fire type move is Overheat so it’s not exactly a sweeper, but its synergistic defensive typing may allow it more leeway than its grass type counterpart has  when it comes to Volt Switching to reset its stats. That better defensive typing also just makes it a better support.
mesprit: Among the three lake pokemon, Mesprit is closer to a Mew or Celebi than its companions. It has a solid spread of stats with 80 hp and 80 speed paired with 105 in every other stat allowing it to function as a bulky support or offensive threat. It has access to a fairly deep pool of coverage attacks, especially on the special side. Its signature move Mystical Power (shared with the other lake pokemon) is a 70 power 90% accurate psychic type attack that also boosts the user’s Special Attack by one stage, giving Mesprit even more reason to be run as a special attacker over a physical one. The 105 attack can feel a bit of a waste, but can still be used in a pinch if needed for a particular match up. Pure psychic typing is less than great, but Mesprit is still well positioned in a draft league with respectable utility. It can set screens and trick room, skill swap the valuable levitate ability, set up with calm mind, or be used as bulky weather setter with respectable damage output. It is definitely worse than Mew and Celebi, but coming somewhat close means it should be considered a strong mid tier pick.
gastrodon: Hello? Is this “The Based Department™”? I have a pokemon here who belongs to you, it’s a bulky water/ground special trick room sweeper with an ability that completely shuts down water types? Yeah, it’s got a base 39 speed so it will always go first in trick room, but its 111 HP, 82 SpD and 68 Def make it hard to kill even outside of trick room if you don’t have a grass type move handy. Right, grass is its only weakness. I’m also seeing here that it gets some good supportive moves like Helping Hand, Yawn, Recover. Toxic, Pain Split, Clear Smog, Acid Armor…. What’s that? It can just sit there and spam Muddy Water and Earth Power if it wants to? Yeah, I guess that’s true. Anyway, I need you to come pick it up by like round 2 or 3 of the draft, it’s really annoying to deal with.
magnezone: Magnezone is a slow, bulky, powerful special attacker with a good typing and ability. Magnezone is fairly simple without many utility options outside of screens and Volt Switch, but its stats and typing help make up for that. Magnezone does have to work around a strong need for speed control and 4x weakness to Ground type attacks, but with a built in focus sash via the Sturdy ability, it should be able to get off meaningful damage fairly consistently. In the right matchups and with the right support, it will be a force to be reckoned with. Magnezone is a mid-to-high tier attacker that demands respect from opposing team builders even if it may die easily to a ground move.
mamoswine: Mamoswine is a strong and bulky physical attacker with poor special defense and moderate speed. Its Ground and Ice typing affords it excellent offensive coverage with which to utilize its strong 130 attack stat. At 80 speed, it isn’t fast enough to naturally outspeed a lot of major threats, but it gets access to STAB Ice Shard for a priority attack, and is an excellent Choice Scarf user or beneficiary of speed control. Its typing makes it well positioned against some of the top threats such as Garchomp and allows it to benefit from the two Snow setters. Mamoswine is a strong high mid-tier option.
porygonz: It has a lot of potential. With 135 special attack and two solid abilities, it has the potential to do some really impressive damage. Potential. Unlike its previous evolution, Z isn’t very bulky. It is fast and hits hard and that’s it. It can hit harder with Adaptability to boost tri-attack into a really hard hitting move or use Download to (maybe) get a special attack boost and use a decent list of coverage moves. With Nasty Plot, it can hit even harder. Porygon-Z hits hard and has the same supportive options that 2 had, just without the bulk. If you need some non-Tailwind speed control, Z has both Icy Wind and Electroweb. It can absolutely round out a team’s offense.
rampardos: Rampardos is a simple pokemon: do big damage. Support is for the weak and defense is for the cowardly; Rampardos embodies the spirit of playing pokemon as a kid where the only number that mattered was power. As such, it is a very difficult pokemon to get working. It is slow. Base 58 speed means tailwind will not help this guy, it needs trick room. But if you can get it inside of ‘trick room’, almost nothing will stand in its way. It has an oddly large list of physical coverage moves including rock blast if you want to run loaded dice (or just like gambling). With 165 base attack it is tied for 10th highest attack of all pokemon. In the limited gen 4 only format, only mega Garchomp beats it and mega Gallade ties it. Simple, straightforward, and powerful.
magmortar: It gets Follow Me! As previously noted, any Pokemon with redirection can only be so bad. Hell, Magmortar is really good! Plus, this isn’t some half-measure like Rage Powder, this is the full, unadulterated original. Outside of the ability Stalwart (which doesn’t exist in Sinnoh), there is no getting around the redirection of Follow Me. Any single-target moves will be diverted into Magmortar. And Magmortar is a great redirection user as both of its abilities help out. Flame Body gives a 30% chance to burn when hit with a contact move, and Vital Spirit prevents it from falling asleep if redirecting a move like Hypnosis or Sleep Powder (Spore is mercifully not learned by any Sinnoh natives). It also has the added benefit of being the fire type thus preventing burns. This means it can tank a Will-O-Wisp and keep a physical attacker safe. Since it can’t use Eviolite, it can’t take quite as well as its previous evolution, but still has decent bulk to stick around. This also means it is free to use a more diverse set of items. Try Safety Goggles to avoid sleep and use Flame Body, use Sitrus Berry to stick around longer, use a type-resist berry, and so on. Even if you aren’t using a supportive set, with a 125 base special attack, you can hit decently hard. The speed stat is a bit awkward and the attacking move pool isn’t very deep, the ability to use Follow Me and use it so well, means this is a great pokemon for any team. It is probably worth a late round 2/ early round 3 get.
electivire: I haven’t seen this pokemon get much use competitively, but it’s not bad by any means. Having Follow Me does, indeed, a good pokemon make. But that’s not all Electivire has going for it, in fact, it’s not even really meant to be a support. Electivire is just a solid, fast physical attacker with a pretty sweet ability in Motor Drive and a generous amount of special bulk. Yeah, Electabuzz is bulkier with Eviolite but it doesn’t really matter all that much. Electivire has the added benefit of its ability making it immune to electric type moves, which does allow it to make great use of Follow Me when protecting a flying or water type partner. Seems it parallels Magmortar yet again in that way. Then you also have Bulk Up, Electroweb, Earthquake, Knock Off, Taunt, even Reflect and Light Screen. Maybe it IS a good support! Just seems like a really versatile pick, perfect for draft league. If it’s available in the 4th or especially 5th round, it’s 100% worth picking up, I think it’d make a good addition to almost any team.
rotomfrost: If you have Froslass or Abomasnow, you would be a fool to sleep on Rotom-Frost. Its unique move is Blizzard, easily the best of the 5 rotom form moves, provided you have a snow setter to enable its accuracy. The fridge can easily get away with several Blizzard blasts with its immense bulk, especially if you enable it further with Aurora Veil. Of course, Ice-electric is by far the worst typing of the 5 defensively so it’s not as good at the typical support role Rotom tends to fill but then, that’s the trade-off.
mismagius: Ah, the Flutter Mane at home. I joke, but the moves and stat spread really are just a toned down Flutter Mane. It has access to a fair number of fun supportive options and at base 105 speed, it is on the faster end of the format. It also hits reasonably hard with a great number of coverage moves. Importantly, it has access to both Trick Room and Imprison. Even if you aren’t shutting down an opponent’s Trick Room, Imprison is great for preventing them from using Protect so it can enable a big damage dealer to run wild. If you get a strong Earthquake user like Garchomp next to it, Levitate keeps you safe while your partner hits everyone else with strong spread damage. Overall: Mismagius is a great support/ damage hybrid which is a great pickup 4th round or later.
drifblim: This pokemon is neato! Firstly, it has a TON of health– tied for 10th highest in Pokemon. It also gets access to Pain Split. Normally, having high health isn’t ideal with Pain Split since you risk giving more HP than you get but it works great when aimed at a teammate to sacrifice some of your health to patch up an ally. With Strength Sap, it can heal back up while weakening a threat and be used as an odd health pack. It gets a myriad of supportive options too, including three forms of speed control: Tailwind, Icy Wind, and Thunder Wave. The hits don’t stop there! It gets Will-O-Wisp, Haze, Hypnosis (let’s go gambling), and so on. There are far dumber supportive options too like Stockpile + Baton Pass. Technically, you can also Baton Pass a Minimize boost but don’t. I will think less of you as a person. With a respectable special attack, it can deal some damage while it supports too. It certainly isn’t on anyone’s mind when you think of a great Pokemon, but it has the potential to be a solid work horse and a thorn in the side of anyone who faces it.
floatzel: Floatzel is a fast physical attacker with access to decent utility options including Icy Wind and Taunt. It’s attack stat is nothing to write home about at 105, but its speed makes up for it somewhat, and fast Taunt is especially helpful. Its hp stat of 85 almost makes up for its terrible defenses, and it would probably be an acceptable if not great special attacker if you really needed it. It is the only swift swim user available in the draft which increases its value somewhat but with no natural rain setters you would ideally need it with a prankster rain setter. Floatzel’s natural speed does mean it usually doesn’t need it and while it isn’t going to carry any teams, Floatzel will very often find a useful role to play. It’s hard for a pokemon this fast to be very bad.
drapion: Drapion is a solid physical attacker with a good stat distribution and typing. Its attack is a moderate 90 which is usable but not overwhelming by any means. It has a high defense of 110 but is somewhat specially frail. It has a speed of 95 which puts it slightly on the faster side, but it won’t outspeed very consistently. Dark+Poison typing leaves it weak to only ground, which is nice because most ground type attackers are physical, where its defenses are pretty good. Unfortunately its abilities are kind of useless, but it gets plenty of strong coverage options and can set itself up with Swords Dance. If you want to gamble with Sniper, you can use Night Slash and Cross Poison alongside a scope lens to roll for big crits, but it obviously will not be consistent. No access to Focus Energy is a bummer. Drapion will be a respectable mid-round pick to add a physical attacker.
abomasnow: I love this guy! If nothing else, look up the cries for both Abomasnow and Snover. Great stuff. Battling? Oh they’re awful. As we have seen with many pokemon in previous seasons: having an easily exploitable weakness typically makes you pretty bad. Abomasnow’s weakness: abysmal typing. These two types, while thematically interesting together, do not play well and basically do nothing for each other. Grass and Ice are both weak defensively and that leaves this poor guy with 7 types which can hit them for super effective damage– fire is even a 4x weakness. Since everyone can counter-team in draft league, be prepared because everyone on your opponent’s team that can, will carry a fire coverage move. It’s a shame too, because if you ignore the typing, Abomasnow has a lot going for it. By the stats, it has surprisingly good bulk. Since it also gets a great ability, Snow Warning, it benefits from the 50% boost in physical defense that ice types get in the snow. Even better, it gets access to Aurora Veil which is both screens rolled into one, so it can provide good support even if it goes down quickly. Offensively, grass/ ice fares much better with only Steel and Fire types resisting both. Since Sinnoh is weird, and dual-types exist, this means only 8 pokemon lines from Sinnoh can’t be hit for neutral with this STAB combination. Those pokemon are: Infernape,Trash Wormadam, Bronzong, Lucario, Magnezone, Magmortar, Rotom Heat, and Heatran (who quad resists both). Not bad. In its mega it gets a lot more stats, but becomes much slower. If you want to make this beast shine, it needs Trick Room support. And that’s the problem. They are too frail to function without Trick Room but setting it up can be a pain. I wish it were better, but I have a feeling that you can pick up this one as a cheap mega in rounds 3 or 4, maybe even later.
yanmega: I want them to give this one a mega evolution so bad, guys. You have no idea how satisfying and funny it would be to me to use Mega Yanmega. Alas, we do not live in that world yet. Yanmega is just a straight upgrade to Yanma. Speed Boost, Tinted Lens, and Frisk are all great abilities. Though, it does not have access to compound eyes, unfortunately. This means Speed Boost is strictly the best bet in most cases. 95 Speed is a good enough starting point but after one turn, you’re off to the races, as it were. This is a viable Tailwind setter who can also supply some impressive damage with 116 Special Attack. Fun fact- Bug Buzz is a sound-based move, so you can actually get some serious value out of Throat Spray on Yanmega, especially when you’re also raising your speed every turn (or hitting resists for neutral with Tinted Lens, as the case may be). But enough glazing. Yanmega is still incredibly killable, what with its 4x weakness to rock you need to watch out for, and its lack of Compound Eyes makes it even less reliable than Yanma at using Hypnosis. Without a solid support option like that, it can sometimes struggle to contribute meaningfully to battle before getting taken out. It does get some good coverage with Shadow Ball, Giga Drain, Ancient Power, and even Solar Beam for some reason. It’s not a bad pokemon and there are a lot worse Tailwind setters out there, but you can probably get away with nabbing it pretty late.
roserade: Now HERE’S a pokemon that can make use of Technician. Roserade is just a great pokemon, through and through. 125 base special attack is nothing to scoff at, and with Technician, Magical Leaf actually becomes a viable damaging move that never misses. Not only that, but Technician on a strong special attacker also makes Roserade one of the best Hidden Power users you’ll ever find. With extra coverage moves like Dazzling Gleam, Shadow Ball, Weather Ball, and Extrasensory, this is one versatile mon. And the cherry on top- Life Dew! Why not? Roserade is also extremely specially bulky, which works out for a grass/poison type whose main weaknesses (fire and psychic) are usually special attackers.
pachirisu: World Champion Pachirisu. It’s good! Seriously! With access to ‘Follow Me’ there is only so bad a pokemon can be! Additionally, it has access to Volt Absorb, meaning it can regain lost HP if the opponent isn’t careful and launches an electric attack carelessly. It has other supportive moves like Charm, to lower attack, Super Fang, for flat damage, and Nuzzle for a great combo of damage and guaranteed paralysis. Nuzzle is especially good since it will break focus sash and inflict paralysis thus cutting the opponent's speed in half (to say nothing of the 25% chance to lose a turn). With a deep list of great supportive options, Pachirisu will fit great on any team. An absolute steal if you can get it 3rd round or later.
tangrowth: Tangrowth is a slow, physically bulky mixed attacker. With 125 defense and 100 hp, it will tank physical attacks very well. Its special defense is its main weakness at only 50. It boasts 100 attack and 110 special attack making it a very passable attacker and special attacker. Tangrowth has a scary arsenal of moves including Sleep Powder, Rage Powder, Leech Seed, Pain Split, and Knock Off on the more supportive side. Tangrowth can set up with Swords Dance or heal itself with Giga Drain. It gets interesting coverage including Poison Jab and Stomping Tantrum. Tangrowth gets Regenerator to help it heal up and can even run Chlorophyll if desired. However, at 50 speed even under sun it may struggle to outspeed the fastest opponents. On the flip side, this makes Tangrowth a powerful Trick Room or anti-Trick Room threat. If there wasn’t as much redirection available, Tangrowth would be more valuable, but it still should do the redirection job quite well on whatever team it lands on.
rotommow: Compared to other Rotom options, Rotom-Mow gains a Grass typing and access to the attack Leaf Storm. The Grass typing gives Rotom a lot of exploitable weaknesses that means it won't be suited to function as a bulky support in the same way as other Rotom Appliance forms. It functions better as an offensive burst pokemon with Leaf Storm dropping special attack and giving it even less staying power. It's probably best paired with a Choice Scarf or Specs and used to burst down specific targets with a Grass weakness.
dusknoir: Dusknoir and Honchkrow should form a support group for pokemon who are outshined by their pre-evolution. The sad thing is if Eviolite didn’t exist, Dusknoir would be a strict improvement on Dusclops. However, because its defenses are only 5 points higher, the Eviolite bonus FAR outweighs that. But enough about that. Dusknoir can still basically do everything Dusclops can do, 135 in both defenses is amazing and it gets 100 base Attack to boot. If they had just given Dusknoir a good ability, it might be better than Dusclops overall, but nah. You’re stuck with Pressure and Frisk. Use Frisk. Dusknoir’s main mode is still as a Trick Room setter/support, but the extra Attack, combined with some good coverage with the elemental punch moves, and Darkest Lariat (which Dusclops doesn’t get) mean it’s a bit more versatile. Who knows? Maybe in the context of draft league, it could end up outshining Dusclops in overall usefulness. Stranger Things™ have happened. Also Dusknoir is a really cool character in Mystery Dungeon so that makes it the bestest pokemon ever.
rhyperior: Rhyperior is kinda hype. If your opponent doesn’t happen to have a good special attacker, it can be hard to deal with this guy. A staggering 140 Attack, 115 HP, and 130 Defense put it a cut above the rest on the physical end of things. It does have only 55 Special Defense though. And unfortunately for Rhyperior, special attacks not only exist, but also tend to come in the form of water or even grass type attacks, both of which it is 4x weak to. Life sure is hard for rock-ground types. However, if you put this bad boy in sandstorm on a team with, say, Hippowdon on it, the 50% Special Defense boost, combined with the ability Solid Rock and perhaps a strategically-chosen berry to reduce super effective damage, it could all come together to compensate for that glaring weakness. The last hurdle to making Rhyperior really pop off would be getting Trick Room up, as its 40 speed makes it pretty hard to use without it. But WITH Trick Room? Uh, yeah, hide your lunch money, kiddos, cuz Rhyperior is here to crack some skulls. Earthquake, Hammer Arm, Heat Crash, Heavy Slam, Rock Slide, Rock Blast, High Horsepower, Body Press, Supercell Damn Slam, I’m just getting started, Superpower, Thunder Punch, Ice Punch, Poison Jab, Megahorn, Aqua Tail, Crunch, Shadow Claw??? You get the picture. No pokemon in the game is safe from this avalanche of coverage moves (it also gets Avalanche, if you were curious). It just needs some help getting where it needs to be. Good pokemon, probably a 4th or 5th rounder. I’d say if you get it in round 6, that’s a really good value.
rotomfan: This is the pick for people who really hate ground types. With all Rotom forms getting the ability, Levitate, and this guy being part flying type, it is immune to ground 2 separate ways. Just throw on an air balloon for extra insurance. Everyone dunks on this form of Rotom but like, it isn’t awful, just probably the worst of all of the appliance forms. Having your ability be completely useless feels pretty bad, but it can still do a lot of the same bulky support stuff that the others can. Will-O-Wisp, Thunder Wave, screens, etc. it still has them. The problem is the added flying type doesn’t really do anything to help out. Cool, you now resist fighting, and bug– call the press. Though it comes at the cost of being weak to both ice and rock, two very strong attacking types. And for the trouble you now get access to Air Slash, a pretty mid attacking move? Again, not bad– just kind of okay.  Flying typing is decent offensive coverage, especially for otherwise frustrating Grass types, but Rotom-Fan still ends up as one of the weaker choices. I would probably predict this thing to be picked up sometime in the 4th maybe 5th round? For a late-round value pick, it will shine but if you don’t get it, you probably aren’t missing much.
bibarel: Bibarel has horrible stats and a fairly uninspiring move pool. It can only realistically function as a physical attacker but it does get access to Yawn, Super Fang, and Taunt. Its ability Simple is quite strong. With 1 swords dance, you can be at +4. Combine this with STAB Aqua Jet and Bibarel could be a real threat. That being said, Bibarel doesn't have the bulk or attack stat to consistently sweep under those conditions. As a late pick for adding a water type, it can do the job.
spiritomb: Spiritomb is so cool! Not widely considered to be a very good pokemon, I think a gen 4 restricted draft league is just the place for this guy to shine. Dark/ghost is fantastic typing, you only have 1 weakness and it’s Fairy, which is pretty good in a format with only one viable fairy type. In most matchups, this means it’s virtually impossible to hit this pokemon for super effective STAB damage, which is just as well for Spiritomb, who is so bulky it’s spOOoOoooOky! 50 HP is bad but not when you also have 108 Defense and Special Defense. Zoo-wee-mama! 35 Speed makes this the ultimate Trick Room support, or even a Trick Room setter if you want. Helping Hand, Disable, Pain Split, Snarl, Taunt, the list goes on. 92 Attack and Special Attack is nothing to write home about but it’s versatile, plus it gets Infiltrator, which could make it useful at dealing damage in certain screen-heavy matchups. Don’t count on it for coverage moves, though. It’s just the standard ghost type spread here. Burning Jealousy does exist though. Anyway, yeah, Spiritomb is awesome. Get it at a bargain in a 5th or 6th round pick and you’ll be sitting pretty.
glaceon: Glaceon is a moderately bulky and fairly slow but powerful special attacker. With its Snow Cloak and Ice Body abilities it is an obvious choice to supplement a Snow focused strategy. Given there are two snow setters in this draft, Glaceon may find itself a priority pick for those players. Its 110 defense will be boosted in snow to high levels, allowing a team builder to focus more points into its special defense. With 130 special attack and access to the rarely distributed Freeze Dry it is a threatening attacker even outside of the typical Blizzard spam. It can disrupt with Yawn or set up with Calm Mind. Even Icy Wind speed control is on the table. Outside of snow, Glaceon may fall a bit flat as its pure Ice typing is somewhat vulnerable defensively, but it should be regarded highly as a pairing for Frosslass or Abomasnow.
infernape: Despite being a personal favorite, Infernape is somewhat awkward as a jack of all trades master of none. Its main strength is in its utility. It has Fake Out, a fairly high speed at 108, equal and respectable special and physical attack at 104 each, and a solid move pool. Taunt, Fake Tears, Coaching and Feint are some highlights. Infernape is likely better in draft league where utility is more valuable than usual, but it will fall short of other more specialized attackers and supports.
lickilicky: Um… it is pretty bulky? It gets a lot of coverage moves? It can Belly Drum? It gets some support options like Icy Wind. Its move pool leans it to a fairly offensive style but it doesn’t have the stats to back that up. 85 attack/ 80 special attack doesn’t inspire confidence. The best it can do is boost up with Swords Dance or Belly Drum then deal some decent damage while sticking around longer than expected. This, if nothing else, means it will have some use. It can almost certainly hit nearly everyone for super effective damage, and maybe pick up a few knock outs against some frail pokemon. The most interesting thing it gets is access to the rare ability: Cloud Nine. If weather setters were more common in Sinnoh, this would be an amazing ability. As it stands, there are 3 weather setters in Sinnoh: Hippowdon, Abomasnow, and Mega Frosslass. It might have a slight niche against teams with any of these Pokemon. Maybe? It will prevent Aurora Veil from going up. That isn’t nothing. Still, it is a very niche pick that will likely not be chosen on purpose but rather that the draft is winding down and you need a 7th round pick.
gliscor: It sure seems like being 4x weak to ice is pretty popular in this generation. However, if you’re gonna pick a 4x weak to ice typing, ground-flying is not a bad choice. Your only other weakness is water and you have a lot of offensive synergy. Gliscor itself isn’t the strongest physical attacker, but it makes up for that fact with incredible bulk. And yeah, you better believe this bad motherfucker gets Swords Dance. You’d better watch out if this thing sets up on you because it’s not gonna be easy to take out if you lack ice type coverage. Gliscor is pretty fast at 95 Speed and can set its own Tailwind. Plus, its rare ability, Poison Heal, allows it to heal ⅛ of its HP every turn when poisoned. Of course, to make use of that, you need a Toxic Orb, which bars you from running Yache Berry like you might want to. And Hyper Cutter is not that great in a format with little to no Intimidate users. Still, Gliscor is a solid pokemon who I think has potential to be vastly underestimated.
torterra: Much like the other gen 4 starters, Torterra is not quite as good as you’d want it to be. It is, however, probably the best of the three. Its ability, shell armor, is only okay, but grass and ground is a pretty good offensive type combo. The two types cover for each other’s weaknesses pretty well, with grass hitting the water types ground is weak to and ground hitting the fire types and poison types that grass may be weak to. However, grass, bug, and flying types pose a pretty big problem for Torterra. That’s to say nothing of its crippling 4x weakness to ice. So what makes this pokemon good? Massive bulk, a solid attack stat, and a pretty usable movepool including Wide Guard, Worry Seed, Wood Hammer, Shell Smash, Headlong Rush, Crunch, and of course, one of the best Earthquakes this side of Garchomp. Basically, it’s just a really good physical attacker, especially in trick room since it has 56 speed. Just be aware of that pesky ice weakness and you have a solid 4th or 5th round pick on your hands. Yache berry is essential.
leafeon: It might be pretty decent? A solid round 4 pick up. There is just a fair bit of grass-type competition and it doesn’t do much to set itself apart from the field. It doesn’t even get access to the standard grass-type powder moves. It does have some nice stats though. Mono-grass isn’t a great defensive typing but with 130 base defense, it should be able to tank a few hits. With a 110 base attack, it should also be able to hit pretty hard in return. While its speed is nothing crazy, it is a fair bit faster than average at 95. Under tailwind, it should be able to outrun most Pokemon in the format. With solid support like Yawn, Wish, and Baton Pass, it can be a pretty decent support. If it goes more offensive, it has access to Swords Dance and two great STAB options in Bullet Seed and Leaf Blade (or Razor Leaf if you want spread damage). While it isn’t flashy, it will likely be a solid pokemon who can help round out a team.
ambipom: Ambipom is fast physical attacker with access to strong utility options, fake-out most notably among them. It also gets moves such as Taunt, Knock-Off, & Brick Break. With Skill Link or Technician it can do respectable damage at a high 115 speed. It’s slightly on the frail side, but not extremely so. You can’t go wrong with a fast fake-out user.
purugly: Purugly is mostly valuable for its quite high speed tier at 112 speed. It has good abilities in Thick Fat and Defiant, but Intimidate (which Defiant is used to counter)  isn’t a super common threat in this generation. Purugly gets Fake Out and solid support options for such a fast pokemon. Charm, Fake Tears, Bulldoze, Knock Off, Taunt, and Super Fang to name a few. It can put up a fast Rain Dance or Sunny Day as well. All that said, Purugly’s other stats are pretty awful. It won’t have staying power with its poor bulk, and its attack stat of 82 means it can’t pump out much damage either. This leaves Purugly as a mid-low tier Fake Out support.
riolu: Riolu is the only Prankster pokemon available in the draft, and that means a lot. It is too frail to make good use of eviolite for the most part, and would more likely hog a focus sash, but the more important question is how good are its support options? The pool is not very diverse but the few options are strong ones. The best bet for Riolu is to spam Coaching onto a bulky and powerful physical attacker. It can also help out with Follow Me redirection, it is the fastest weather setter with both Rain Dance and Sunny Day, can use Quick Guard to shut down priority attacks from opposing pokemon, and has its own priority moves in Quick Attack, Vacuum Wave, and Bullet Punch for breaking opposing Focus Sash. Pairing Riolu with the right partners is pretty crucial to making it truly work, but it shouldn’t be hard to find a good one. Riolu is a solid high to mid tier support.
empoleon: Damn, this one hurts. As a certified Empoleon enjoyer™, I really wanted this one to be good. Unfortunately, Empoleon is stuck being a worse Milotic across the board. It not only has a less efficient base stat spread, wasting more in the lower physical attack, but it is less bulky, slower, has an additional weakness and has fewer stats overall. Granted, the bulk isn’t awful considering how great steel is as a defensive type; that one extra weakness is balanced by gaining a TON of extra resistances. ‘Competitive’ is also still a great ability even if there are far fewer pokemon with intimidate in gen 4. It is also unfortunate given its move pool. Most of the moves you would want use its lower physical attack stat and it gets access to swords dance but not nasty plot. The special move options aren’t great, mostly just the standard water pokemon moves. It gets access to very few supportive options but notably gets access to the rare move ‘Snowscape.’ If you are building a snow-based team, this could be an option. Overall, Empoleon is simply outclassed as a tank, as a support, and as a damage dealer. As a late round pick up, it is usable but not worth anything above 5th round.
toxicroak: Toxicroak is my personal favorite Pokemon, but that doesn’t make it especially good. It has underwhelming stats with 85 speed putting it in an awkward speed tier, and 106 attack not making it too powerful of an offensive threat. Despite that, Toxicroak has an incredibly deep move pool full of strong supportive and offensive options alongside a very good ability in Dry Skin. Some of the highlights include Fake Out, Sucker Punch, and Taunt. Toxicroak gets tons more though including Swords Dance, Super Fang, Baton Pass, Encore, Icy Wind, Helping Hand, and Coaching. Toxicroak has many coverage and utility attacks including Brick Break, Knock Off, Drain Punch, Throat Chop, Bullet Punch, and elemental punches. You could do a lot worse for a Fake Out Pokemon, and I doubt Toxicroak will fall much further than the 4th or 5th round.
luxray: Luxray is a super cool pokemon but from a competitive angle it's just somewhat lacking. It has a great ability in Intimidate as well as access to Guts to boost its powerful 120 attack stat. Where it falls short is in movepool, bulk, and speed. At 70 speed, Luxray is slow but not slow enough for Trick Room in most cases. Its 80 hp & 79 def/spdef stats don't give it enough bulk to be difficult to remove. It is stuck using its high attack stat to use Supercell Slam or Thunder Fang for its only physical STAB options. Its support move pool is largely uninspiring and its poor bulk and speed make it hard to use anyhow. Unlike previous generations, the pool of Electric types isn't nearly thin so it's not in a unique position there either. Overall it isn't useless, most gen 4 pokemon aren't, but it will be a niche pick I wouldn't expect to bring every week.
hippowdon: Hey, weren’t we just talking about this guy? I really like Hippowdon. The only other Sand Stream user of all time besides Tyranitar, Hippowdon is gonna be pretty valuable in a generation with a lot of rock types and no Tyranitar. I mentioned how good Garchomp is on a sand team in the Garchomp dissertation I wrote but there’s also Rampardos, Rhyperior, Bastiodon, Probopass, and plenty more rock/ground/steel types that wouldn’t mind a sand setter like this one. Plus, it’s always good to have a switch-in that shuts down someone’s weather-based strategy. Unfortunately for Hippowdon, the other weather setters in this generation do kinda fuck it up, those being Abomasnow and Froslass. But anyway, Hippowdon is a physically bulky, decently strong physical attacker a la Torterra, but without a 4x weakness, as it’s a mono ground type. 47 speed makes it pretty good in Trick Room and its 118 defense makes it decent at using Body Press (but it does not get Iron Defense). This pokemon is sadly a bit of a jack of all trades master of none type (a la Infernape) and there are other pokemon who do what it does better (a la Empoleon) but it does get a wide pool of coverage moves and can heal itself with Slack Off, as well as put opponents to sleep with Yawn. Plus, it gets Helping Hand, which makes it a fantastic partner to Garchomp. It’s a very useful Pokemon and should not be slept on. Easy 3rd round pick.
regigigas: I know it. You know it. Let’s just get it out of the way now. This mother fucker gets Slow Start, everyone point and laugh. It is a tragedy though. With 160 base attack, 100 base speed, and 110 in all of HP, defense, and special defense it has a great stat line. But Slow Start cuts that attack and speed in half for the first 5 turns it is on the field and it resets every time it switches out. God hates this Pokemon. The only way it can function is with a partner who knows Gastro Acid, or Worry Seed to get rid of this awful ability. If you can unshackle this monster, it can absolutely win games. Getting it going might be worth it, but by the time you get it out of bed, you might already be too far behind to salvage the match. A high risk/ high reward Pokemon destined to languish in rounds 4 and 5.
carnivine: Damn, this Pokemon can really click Rage Powder and die. I joke, mostly. From past seasons, I have learned the value of even just a few good supportive options and how tanky a pokemon can be when fully invested that way. While you aren’t likely to do much damage, 100 base attack is respectable enough to do decent chip to anyone who ignores you. But you aren’t here for damage. Rage powder is good. Redirection is good. It is so good that even classically bad pokemon can be usable with redirection and a touch of bulk. Carnivine isn’t by any means a tank, but the bulk is usable. The other supportive options are pretty limited. I guess you can do something with the ability suppression of Gastro Acid, especially if you have Regigigas on your team. Sleep powder is good, if unreliable. But because Carnivine is widely seen as a bad pokemon you can likely pick it up for a great deal. I predict that Carnivine will be a slight sleeper pick– an immensely usable Pokemon floating somewhere in the later rounds. Even if all it does it spam Rage Powder, that can often be enough to win a game or two.
cherrim: Cherrim is one of the Pokemon ever created. I’m actually really interested to see if this pokemon gets much use in this draft league because it has some unique things it can do but I’ve never really heard anyone talk about it much at all in a competitive context. So, the main gimmick with Cherrim is its signature ability Flower Gift, which changes its form in the sun and gives itself and all its allies a 1.5x Special Defense AND Attack boost. I suppose that makes it a really good support, but we don’t have any drought users in this pool so making use of it may prove a bit difficult. Besides, the only drought users that exist are special attackers, so the Attack boost is only so valuable. Prankster Sunny Day is also not ideal because Cherrim itself is a Special Attacker, and anyone with the ability Prankster is bound to be weak offensively. This leaves Cherrim with the unfortunate burden of needing to set its own sun for your team to get the most out of its ability. At 85 speed though, it’s not unreasonable that you might be able to benefit from that boost within the same turn of setting it up. Plus, everything I just said only pertains to the Attack boost side of it, the Special Defense boost cannot be overlooked, that’s extremely valuable. That’s essentially a free Assault Vest for the whole team as long as Cherrim is on the field. It is highly conditional, though. It’s certainly no Friend Guard. Cherrim also gets the extremely rare (but just as useless) move Flower Shield, which raises the defense of all grass types by 1. Um…cool! Yeah, aside from that, there’s not much more to say about Cherrim. Its stats are aggressively mediocre across the board and its movepool is only okay. Helping Hand and Pollen Puff are really the main ways it can contribute to battle after setting sun. But I have a feeling you’re always gonna want the same 4 moves- Sunny Day, Helping Hand, Pollen Puff, and Protect. I can think of better supports but I can think of worse ones too. I’ve never seen a pokemon like Cherrim though. I’m excited to see what it can do.
lumineon: Oh my God, Lumineon gets Storm Drain? What the hell? It also gets Swift Swim, wow! Those are some really good abilities, this pokemon must be awesome! *Looks inside* Oh, that’s…. That’s 69 Attack and Special Attack… Okay so, fast bulky support? Totally, totally, we’ve got Tailwind, Helping Hand, Icy Wind, and… and…. Oh, that’s it…. Huh. It’s no wonder Lumineon is famously the least famous pokemon of all time. Like I’m sorry man, Storm Drain is a great ability but you have to actually DO something too. Your competition is GASTRODON, man. Step it up.
honchkrow: Honchkrow will forever live in Murkrow’s shadow as it lacks the broken Prankster ability and is arguably less bulky due to its 52 base defensive stats and no access to eviolite. What it gets in return is a very high 100 base HP and respectable 125 Attack and 105 Special Attack, meaning it can kind of function as a split attacker. Things once again get worse for it though, as its 71 base speed leaves it in the ultimate awkward spot, being way too fast for trick room, but way too slow to function without Tailwind, which it wants to be the one setting. Woof. At the end of the day, what you see is what you get with Honchkrow. If you need a strong flying/dark type, it will get the job done. It won’t go down in one hit and it will deal some good damage with a Knock- oh, sorry, it doesn’t get Knock-Off….uh, it will deal some good damage with a Sucker Punch or….Lash Out? Man… I mean, Brave Bird and and Acrobatics exist, so it’s one of the better flying type attackers out there. Staraptor does all of that better, though. It has the same wide supportive move pool Murkrow has so it’s still good enough but it’s like a 7th rounder.
skuntank: Appropriately, it kind of stinks. It can do more than nothing, which is better than some pokemon this generation. It can act as an annoying tank. With a respectable HP and workable defensive stats, it should be able to take a hit pretty well. This is aided by its dark/poison typing leaving it with only one weakness and four resistances and an immunity. The speed stat leaves a lot to be desired since it is too fast for Trick Room, but too slow to work outside of tailwind. If you use Skunktank as a bulky support, you’re likely going to find more success, even if the supportive options aren’t very deep. It gets both Toxic and Fire Spin, if you want to slowly chip down a foe, but it also gets Taunt and the decently reliable Super Fang. It can set weather but with its speed, it likely won’t be very good at that. The best move it gets is likely Acid Spray which can chip to break a Focus Sash, and it lowers Special Defense by 2 stages. It also gets Snarl,  a spread move which lowers Special Attack by 1 for everyone it hits. To make this a bit better, Skuntank also gets the ability Stench, which adds a flat 10% flinch chance to every move which doesn’t already have a flinch chance. Before you think this is good, remember that flinch only matters if you can move before the opponent. Also, the flinch chance can’t be boosted by holding King’s Rock or Razor Fang, and using a multi-hit move doesn’t give you more flinch chances. Still, giving Snarl a slight chance to flinch on top of the stat drop is decent. If you have a team with a slow, tanky playstyle, you might find room for Skuntank. More likely, you will just draft this pokemon in the late rounds and maybe use it once.
probopass: Damn. What a tragic pokemon. Everyone thinks they’re bulky until the two, 4x weaknesses walk in. Even with maxed out defenses, it will still fall to most STAB fighting or ground-type moves. That low 60 base HP is also not doing it any favors. Even weaker attacks like Mach Punch will still likely do 30-40%. If you get lucky and the opponent doesn’t run any fighting or ground type moves, it might work as a wall. It gets Body Press, which is nice. Unfortunately it doesn’t hit very hard so it can’t take advantage of Sturdy’s survival boon. It is also too slow to avoid being doubled and killed before it can attack. Just not a good pokemon. I love the mustache though.
vespiquen: I can almost see what they were trying to do when they made Vespiquen, but “trying” is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that statement. Vespiquen is designed as a slow, bulky pokemon with mixed physical and special offenses. It can use unique “Order” moves to boost its defenses, heal itself, and attack with a 90 power STAB attack with increased crit rate. This could almost work, except Bug-Flying typing has 5 weaknesses including common types like Fire, Ice, and Electric as well as a 4x weakness to Rock which really hurts due to how powerful Rock Slide is in doubles. All that said, Vespiquen at least has a concept of a plan for how it should be used. It is slow enough to work in Trick Room, and it can set Tailwind if you want. It has decent coverage options with moves like Sludge Bomb and Power Gem. Pick it late.
bastiodon: Bastiodon is the slowest non-mega in the format and its bulk is immense. However, its offensive stats are so pathetic, you aren't likely to be able to do much for damage outside of Iron Defense + Body Press, and that's super predictable. Also your typing leaves you with two 4x weaknesses to common types. That leaves you stuck doing supportive moves which you don't have amazing options for. Wide Guard, Sunny Day and Rain Dance, Reflect, and Taunt are key options. But after that you don't have much. Screech and Metal Sound? Not very inspiring. You could spam fissure which would be really funny if it worked, but not exactly a pokemon you want to play around. I would only take bastiodon in the absolute latest rounds of the draft.
kricketune: Waiter! Oh, waiter! I’m afraid you forgot to bring me my stats! I assure you, I most certainly did not order a 384 base stat total with 65 speed and 85 attack as my only means of offense. There must be some mistake here. I see you brought me the Technician ability I asked for, but there must be more I can do with it than simply using Bug Bite, Powerup Punch, and Aerial Ace. My 51 base defenses cannot sustain moves like that. Surely, this establishment must offer some priority moves. No? Ok, can I at least see a support menu then? Hmmm…. Perish Song…Taunt….Toxic…..Sticky Web….and….Baton Pass?! That’s all?! Well, pardon my saying so, but I’ll be taking the check please! And I shan’t be dining here again any time soon! Harrumph!
bronzor: Wow, it's Bronzong at home! Well... that might be a little harsh. As a pre-evolution, this pokemon has access to eviolite, bringing its defenses to nearly 130! That beats out Bronzong at 116, and it's slower, too, which makes it outspeed nearly everything in Trick Room. However, it has no offenses to speak of and is always moves last outside of Trick Room, so it can be a bit of a lame duck if gets taunted or doesn't have a strong partner next to it.
snover: Well, it's got snow warning. That's... kinda cool I guess...
sableye: Here we have a pokemon who I would describe as very good. Sableye is one of the 2 prankster pokemon available in this gen, the other being Riolu, and even though Sableye doesn’t get access to tailwind, it makes up for it by getting just about every other support move you could possibly want. Fake out, rain dance, sunny day, gravity, quash, screens, disable, encore, taunt, you name it. Sableye is also unique in that its mega enables an entirely different playstyle, getting incredibly bulky and gaining the ability Magic Bounce, allowing it to suddenly become a wall if you need it to. Maybe not how I would use it but good to have as an option depending on the matchup. Any team would benefit from Sableye.
ludicolo: Very good pokemon, solid option for filling out any rain team. That’s mainly because it’s a bulky water type with swift swim, fake out, and encore. Fake out is usually reserved for frail pokemon, so it’s always good when a bulky pokemon like ludicolo can use it. But swift swim paired with encore can be extremely disruptive as well, and ludicolo can do respectable enough damage in addition to that to where it becomes a pretty annoying presence.
milotic: This stupid-ass snake pisses me off and in this case that’s actually a really good thing. Here’s why- Milotic is especially tuned to being a ridiculously tanky, supportive wall that can and will last oodles and oodles of turns on the field, even if you’re consistently targeting it. Its ability Competitive allows it to counter intimidate users and generally be tricky to deal with. A vast supportive movepool allows you to tool it towards whatever your team needs, be it healing from life dew, potential burns from scald, speed control with icy wind, screens, accuracy drops from muddy water, or the very best and most obnoxious mode- coil + hypnosis! Milotic is the most iconic leftovers user of all time, and if you also give it Recover, killing it will be a monumental pain in the ass. Highly recommend.
chimecho: What’s up, guys, Cart Mart here. This is my number one favorite pokemon of all time and I’m so happy to report that it’s finally viable in VGC! This is thanks entirely to its new mega form, which is absolutely essential for making this pokemon work. Base Chimecho is mainly held back by its stats, which aren’t abysmal by any means, but not good enough to enable it to be the slow support it was clearly designed to be. The singular ability levitate giving it an incidental immunity to ground is a big missed opportunity. Other psychic type supports have abilities that enable them to contribute a lot more to battle, meaning Chimecho has long been outshined and outclassed by better pokemon with more specialized roles. Mega Chimecho, on the other hand, is the powerful generalist Chimecho always dreamed of being. It gets the added steel typing, as well as 30 extra defense and special defense and 40 extra special attack. This makes up for its middling 75 HP and allows it to become a serious threat as a special trick room sweeper, especially thanks to the addition of STAB flash cannon (which is a valuable answer to the many powerful fairy and ice type megas). It still only has the ability Levitate, but now that it’s a steel type, it actually benefits from that ability far more than it did before. It basically becomes a much stronger version of Bronzong, with a similarly wide array of supportive moves to choose from. Mega Chimecho’s extra bulk makes it much better at setting up with Calm Mind, which can quickly make it extremely threatening, plus it can restore its own health with Recover, heal its allies with Heal Pulse, set its own trick room, supply some speed control with icy wind, trip people up with Ally Switch, infuriate foes with taunt and encore, even pass Levitate onto another pokemon with Skill Swap or Entrainment. For more niche options, consider Heal bell if you’re worried about a physical attacker getting burned, or gravity + hypnosis for maximum cheese. Chimecho even gets Boomburst now, which is a 140 base power special normal type spread move (that also hits your ally). Basically, this pokemon is cracked now. It has tools for just about any situation and can contribute to just about any team, even if trick room is the most obvious mode to use it in. It isn’t totally necessary. Obviously, its base form being as mediocre as it is still holds it back. You’ll usually be sacrificing much stronger megas if you choose Chimecho, but stronger doesn’t mean better, and Mega Chimecho’s balance of strength, bulk, and supportive versatility make it genuinely one of the best Pokemon I’ve ever used. Take my word with 0 grains of salt, as I am completely unbiased and objective.
gardevoir: Gardevoir is a pretty strong psychic/fairy special attacker with extremely lopsided defenses- 115 SpD and only 65 Def. That physical defense deficiency is not solved by its mega evolution (nor is its measly 68 HP), but it hardly matters because mega gardevoir is an absolute powerhouse. 165 special attack and the ability pixilate allow her to unleash absolutely devastating hyper voices that can shred an unprepared team to dust. You can’t go wrong with gardevoir on your team. It’s a respectable pokemon with or without mega, as its base form has some decent abilities in trace and telepathy. Just be wary that its speed stat (80) leaves something to be desired and it’s a bit too frail to survive long without some speed control.
camerupt: Camerupt is very slow, moderately bulky, and hits decently hard on both the physical and special side. Its typing is great for offensive coverage and leaves it weak to only water and ground. I wouldn't feel bad about having this pokemon on any trick room team and it's great in sun as well. The movepool includes yawn and eruption as well as a smattering of physical and special fire and ground attacks. Earth Power is especially nice. Solid rock is a nice ability that gives you just a little bit of extra bulk against super effective moves, and if you pick camerupt with a frost breath user you can turn it into an ABSOLUTE BEAST with Anger Point. Camerupt’s mega form is extraordinarily slow and bulky and will hit very hard with Sheer Force. It is likely to be a potent trick room attacker but not capable of much outside of a trick room setting.
swellow: Swellow is one of the rare flying types WITHOUT Tailwind access (PSA!! THIS IS FALSE!!!!). Despite this, Swallow’s incredible 125 speed combined with Guts and a decent 85 attack stat make Swellow a respectable threat. It is lacking the move pool required to support really any other options, and its defenses are poor. It can use substitute, and rain and sun. Despite being one-dimensional, it will hit pretty hard and fast with Brave Bird.
zangoose: Zangoose is an odd one. In a classic Gen3 move, you are strong, fast, and frail. 115 attack is one of the higher ones we’ve seen so far and 90 speed is a bit above the more commonly seen 80. Zangoose has access to strong moves such as Facade, Final Gambit, Knock-off, and Close Combat as well as some unexpected coverage options like Poison Jab, Zen Headbutt, and Seed Bomb. You get utility from Rock Slide and Brick Break and can set up with Swords Dance. Support isn’t this Pokemon’s forte but you do get helping hand, Taunt, and icy wind in a pinch. I think the selling point of Zangoose is to use its guts-lite Toxic Boost ability to poison yourself and then attack pretty hard with the 115 attack stat. Like a faster, weaker Ursaring.
